item.title: Web application for retrospective geomagnetic storm detection, main phase analysis and identification of solar wind influence on storm intensity
item.description: arXiv:2610.41217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a web application for retrospective detection and analysis of geomagnetic storms using hourly Dst and solar wind data from OMNIWeb. The application detects storm events, identifies their main phases, computes solar wind derived parameters during the main phase, and examines their relationship with storm intensity. Its detection and main phase identification parameters are user-adjustable, allowing different assumptions to be tested interactively rather than imposed through a single fixed parameter set. The analysis covers the period from 1964 through May 2026. Using the default parameter set, 1796 storms with Dst_min <= -50 nT were detected, including 1422 moderate storms (-100 < Dst_min <= -50 nT), 347 intense storms (-250 < Dst_min <= -100 nT), and 27 super-storms (Dst_min <= -250 nT). After filtering for reliable main phase identification, 1643 storms were retained. The average main phase duration per class was 9.25 hours for moderate storms, 11.30 hours for intense storms and 13.75 hours for super-storms. After also requiring OMNIWeb solar wind data availability, 990 storms remained for examining the relationship between storm intensity and solar wind derived parameters over the main phase. The strongest correlations with |Dst_min| were obtained for peak dawn-dusk electric field (Eyp: R = 0.836), peak southward IMF (Bzp: R = -0.811), and integrated electric field (Eyi: R = 0.759). These results are consistent with the importance of the solar wind electric field and southward interplanetary magnetic field in geomagnetic storm development. All outputs are downloadable for further user-defined analysis.
item.dc:creator: Daniil Papakonstantinou (Department of Physics, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Athens, Greece), Ioannis A. Daglis (Department of Physics, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Athens, Greece)

item.title: Equipartition between Alfv\'enic turbulence and energetic ions as the origin of the -5 common spectrum in the heliosphere
item.description: arXiv:2610.40925v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Suprathermal ion tails throughout the heliosphere follow a ``common spectrum,'' $f(v)\propto v^{-5}$. We show that scale-by-scale equipartition between strong Alfv\'enic turbulence and the ions it accelerates predicts both this exponent and the absolute amplitude, $F(v)=B^2/(16\pi^3 m_i v^5)$, with no free parameters. The prediction agrees within a factor of a few with ACE and Voyager 1 spectra across three decades in magnetic energy. We argue that this saturated level is reached where strong turbulence accelerates particles locally; quiet-time tails lie well below it, consistent with nonlocal acceleration.
item.dc:creator: Stanislav Boldyrev, Daniel Humphrey, Vadim Roytershteyn

item.title: Spectroscopic observations of periodic bursty ejections during a dome-spire-shaped jet
item.description: arXiv:2610.41343v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Context: The study investigates the complexity of the formation and evolution of a dome-spire-shaped jet (or anemone jet) that originated in an active region and was presumably driven by null-point magnetic reconnection. Aims: We aim to provide a quantitative estimation of multi-temperature plasma dynamics and physical parameters of the jet and its blob-like features, together with its temporal evolution in three-dimensional perspective. Methods: For this, we analyze unique sit-and-stare spectral (Si IV, Mg II k, and C II) and slit-jaw imaging 1400 {\AA} and 2796 {\AA} observations obtained with the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), with a slit uniquely positioned just above the assumed reconnection site. Co-observations taken with the Fast Imaging Solar Spectrograph of the Goode Solar Telescope in the chromospheric H$\alpha$ and Ca II 8542.10 {\AA} lines were also analyzed. These data are complemented by EUV imaging information from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory. Results: The IRIS observations reveal that the jet is formed by multiple periodic ($\sim$30 s) plasma ejections with blob-like appearance, each associated with strongly blueshifted Si IV 1402.77 {\AA} transition-region emission reaching about $-300$ km/s. More importantly, the ejections are grouped into well-defined packets, each lasting approximately 3--5 min. In contrast, only a single Doppler component is observed in the chromospheric Ca II line. Multi-Gaussian decomposition of the Si IV line profiles reveals a highly accelerated plasma, with line-of-sight speed toward the observer increasing linearly from $\sim$30 to 112 km/s over 66 s, corresponding to an acceleration of 1.3 km/s$^2$. The kinetic energy release rate is estimated in the range of $\sim$1.0$\times10^{24}$--1.0$\times10^{25}$ erg\,s$^{-1}$.
item.dc:creator: Heesu Yang, Maria S. Madjarska, Kyoung-Sun Lee, Klaus Galsgaard

item.title: Relative Influence of Coronal Properties of CME in their Evolution and Geo-effectiveness
item.description: arXiv:2610.41376v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Uncertainties in the coronal mass ejection (CME) properties near the Sun remain a major challenge for accurate space weather forecasting. Understanding the sensitivity of CME evolution to the initial parameters is therefore essential for improving the predictions. We investigate the influence of physical CME properties prescribed at 0.1 AU on their subsequent heliospheric propagation and geoeffectiveness at Earth, using the SWASTi framework. We perform a systematically sampled ensemble of 400 global magnetohydrodynamic simulations by varying the initial CME density, speed, magnetic flux and temperature. We quantify the relative influence of these parameters on CME evolution, plasma properties at L1, and the resulting geomagnetic response. The analysis reveals a clear hierarchy of influence: initial speed primarily controls the peak radial velocity and arrival time at L1, magnetic flux controls the magnetic-field strength, and density governs the peak density and magnetopause compression. Primary parameters account for only half the output variance, highlighting the collective influence of other parameters. Density exhibits the broadest influence across the analyzed outputs. We find a mean arrival-time sensitivities of 2.43h per 100 km/s variation in injection speed and 1.99h per $10^{-18}$ kg/m$^3$ variation in injection density. The CME volume exhibits a two-phase evolution, characterized by an initial gradual expansion followed by a power-law regime with a median expansion index of 2.38. These results establish parameter-specific priorities for CME forecasting, highlighting the importance of constraining CME speed for arrival-time prediction, density for duration and pressure-driven effects, and magnetic flux for geomagnetic response at Earth.
item.dc:creator: Jithu J Athalathil, Asif M Mandayapuram, Prateek Mayank, Bhargav Vaidya

item.title: Accelerating Computation and Resolving Extraneous Roots in the Kinetic Plasma Dispersion Relation Solver BO
item.description: arXiv:2610.41450v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Kinetic dispersion relations are widely used to study waves and instabilities in space, astrophysical, and laboratory plasmas. Iterative root searches depend on initial guesses and may fail to converge or miss important branches. The BO/PDRK solvers [Comput. Phys. Commun. 244, 343-371 (2019)] use rational pole expansions to transform the nonlinear dispersion relation into a matrix eigenvalue problem, obtaining all roots of the approximated relation in one calculation. However, high cyclotron harmonics enlarge the matrix and slow computation, while extraneous roots are difficult to separate from physical modes. We develop BO-T (BO-Tian), an improved version of BO combining two methods. First, for matrix reduction, BO-T applies rank factorization to combined residue matrices, preserving the rational dispersion relation and accounting for the removed pole eigenvalues. Second, for root screening, BO-T uses contour comparison between approximate and reference kinetic dispersion matrices along a closed contour enclosing no poles. This provides a sufficient condition for preserving local root counts, with error bounds for isolated roots and criteria for growth rate signs. Benchmarks on representative electrostatic and electromagnetic cases show speedups of about 10 to 140 for matrix assembly and eigenvalue calculation, exceeding 30 in most cases with high cyclotron harmonics. Root screening recovers the main unstable branches in agreement with published and archived dispersion curves.
item.dc:creator: Xizhi Tian, Huasheng Xie, Long Wei

item.title: Inferring dominant acceleration mechanisms using the longitudinal spread of solar particle intensities: 28 May 2021 event
item.description: arXiv:2610.41749v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Solar energetic particles (SEPs) are typically accelerated during solar eruptions and propagate along magnetic field lines in the inner heliosphere. These eruptions include shock waves driven by coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and magnetic reconnection in solar flares. Disentangling these source mechanisms within the measurements has been a long-standing problem for space physics researchers. Since spacecraft rarely reach the acceleration regions close to the Sun, measured SEP intensities reflect a combination of particle acceleration and interplanetary transport. The method used in this study attempts to identify which of the two main acceleration processes is more dominant for specific particle energies and species in a standalone event. Through this approach, we aim to better identify the signatures associated with these two acceleration phenomena and recognize similar behaviors in measurements with transport effects. This study characterizes the longitudinal spread of the SEP event on 28 May 2021 by fitting Gaussian curves at regular time intervals to particle intensities as a function of spacecraft position. This evolution offers unprecedented detail compared to earlier peak-focused studies, which were also limited to only three observers, while we now benefit from a novel fleet. To support the interpretation of the evolving profiles, we use a 2D SEP transport model to test if the evolution of the SEP distribution can also be caused by interplanetary effects. For this event, we find that the particle distribution of 0.1 MeV electrons remains static, while for 14 and 32 MeV protons, the distribution grows and moves to the west. We suggest that the CME-driven shock is the dominant source for protons, and that the flare is the dominant source only for the studied 0.1 MeV electrons. Interplanetary transport processes could also be contributing to the moving particle distributions.
item.dc:creator: Jaclyn T. Lang, R. Du Toit Strauss, Jan Gieseler, Stefan Jensen, J. Grant Mitchell, Rami Vainio, Nina Dresing

item.title: Current Sheets and Magnetic Reconnection statistics by Solar Orbiter at few to tens of Ion Inertial Lengths I: Energy Dissipation
item.description: arXiv:2610.41923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we study the turbulent origin of ion-scale Current Sheets (CSs) and the dissipation of energy via magnetic reconnection. We analyze 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ ion data from Solar Orbiter, collected between July 2020 and September 2022. We apply an automatic detection algorithm that finds current sheets (CSs) of thickness (length in the normal direction, $\lambda$) near the ion inertial length ($\delta_i$), and classifies them as Alfv\'enic or reconnecting. We compile a catalog of 974 CSs of thickness in the range of few to 90 ion inertial lengths, of which 53 contain an ion reconnection jet. We estimate that Solar Orbiter spends $\sim 1 \%$ of the dwell time inside a CS of few to 90 $\delta_i$ thickness, and 0.06\% inside a reconnecting CS of the same thickness range. By comparing these results with previous studies we estimate that the abundance of CSs and of Reconnecting CSs evolves with heliocentric distance ($r$) as $r^{-0.9}$ and $r^{-1.5}$, respectively. We estimate that magnetic reconnection dissipates $\epsilon_{rec}\sim 30 \hspace{5pt} \text{J} \text{kg}^{-1} \text{s}^{-1},$ in the $\sim 1 - 40$ $\delta_i$ scale-range, by assessing the amount of plasma that interacts with a reconnection exhaust. We show how the dissipation of turbulence energy cascade by magnetic reconnection at scales smaller than 90 $\delta_i$ is more effective closer to the Sun, and decays as $r^{-3.6}$. The current density of Alfv\'enic CSs thicker than the ion inertial length presents scale invariance, obeying $J_0/J_A=0.9(\lambda/2\delta_i)^{-0.71}$, suggesting that CSs generated locally from solar wind turbulence.

item.title: On the curlometer measurement of field-aligned and perpendicular currents in low Earth orbit: Swarm observations and whole geospace simulations
item.description: arXiv:2604.18553v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Measuring field-aligned currents (FACs) using magnetic field observations provides a powerful means to probe the multi-scale interactions between the magnetosphere, ionosphere and thermosphere. In this study, we benchmark the curlometer technique using Swarm spacecraft observations and simulations of the coupled magnetosphere-ionosphere system. We begin by correlating current density curlometer estimates derived from Swarm tetrahedra with varying spatial scales and barycentre locations. This confirms an apparent departure from stationarity for FACs at spatio-temporal scales below 100 km where measurements appear highly uncorrelated. We then analyse simulated magnetic perturbations, where four-point measurements can always be constructed. This shows how, even at meso-scales of hundreds of kilometres, time-shifted FAC estimates can diverge significantly from this ground truth. In both observational and simulated data we find poor tetrahedral configurations can produce spurious perpendicular currents due to numerical instability in the inversion process. This can be mitigated using appropriate quality metrics and high-quality FAC reconstructions still achieved with a tetrahedral face well-aligned to the local magnetic field. These results highlight the dynamic nature of FACs at large as well as small scales, and underscore the substantial advantages of true four-point observations for their accurate analysis.
item.dc:creator: R Gajewski, RT Desai, B Hnat, D Lin, MW Dunlop, M Fillion, G Hulot, Shreedevi P R, M-T Walach, E Panov, J-M Leger, T Jager, D Fischer, W Magnes, JA Blake, T Etchells

item.title: Solar Magnetic Configuration Control over Radiation Belt Electrons
item.description: arXiv:2608.28309v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Earth is surrounded by two highly dynamic concentric belts of particle radiation. The outer radiation belt exhibits coherent variability at solar-cycle, seasonal, and 27-day (Carrington) timescales. While the solar-cycle and Carrington variations have been attributed to the recurrence of coronal hole solar wind, the seasonal variation has long been explained by local geometric effects that modulate the solar wind-magnetosphere coupling. Here, we challenge this paradigm by showing that the periodic recurrence of coronal hole solar wind likewise drives the seasonal variation. We further demonstrate that the Alfv\'enic nature of this solar wind is a key driver of the observed electron flux enhancement in the outer radiation belt. These findings provide a unifying framework linking solar magnetic topology, solar wind properties, and magnetospheric dynamics across multiple timescales at Earth and beyond.
item.dc:creator: Ahmad Lalti, Jonathan Rae, Clare Watt, Stephanie Yardley, Savvas Raptis
